concept_name: Work Done by a Constant Force — W = F·d·cos θ
source_book: NCERT Class 11 Physics Ch.6 Work, Energy and Power, §6.3 Work — table-of-contents scope only, teaching authored from first principles. The atomic concept: work done by a constant force is W = F·d·cos θ — the force magnitude, the displacement it acts through, and only the component of the force along that displacement. Covers the joule as the unit, the zero-work no-displacement case, and the cos θ resolution for 0° <= theta < 90°. Does NOT cover the sign taxonomy of work across all three angle regimes (positive vs negative vs zero work, theta = 90 deg, friction's negative work, the normal force's zero work — all deferred to positive_negative_zero_work, concept #2), kinetic energy (#3), the work-energy theorem (#4), or power (#11/#12). Built on the newtons_laws_body field_3d engine extended with the SEAM K/L/M/N energy layer (docs/loop_runs/ch6_state.md), pure configuration, zero renderer edits (0d).

real_world_anchor.primary: A rolling suitcase pulled by its tilted handle. The hand pulls along the slanted handle, but the case moves horizontally along the floor — the pull and the motion point in different directions, and only the along-the-floor part of the pull moves the case. That is W = F·d·cos θ acting in the student's own hand, on every syllabus, in every country.
real_world_anchor.secondary: Pushing against a stalled car that does not move. Arms shaking, fully tired — the physics work done on the car is exactly zero, because it moved zero distance.

formulas.definition: W = F·d·cos θ — work done by a constant force = force magnitude × displacement magnitude × the cosine of the angle between them
formulas.normal: N = mg − F·sin θ — the pull's vertical component changes the floor's normal reaction
formulas.along_component: F∥ = F·cos θ — only this component lies along the motion and does work
formulas.static_ceiling: f_s = F·cos θ, valid only while F·cos θ ≤ μₛN
formulas.acceleration: a = F·cos θ / m — frictionless states only (S1, S3, S4, S5, S6)

constraints: W = F*d*cos(theta) at all times -- the engine's live work ledger and the formula agree to the last printed digit (SEAM N verified this on the 40N/30deg case)
N = m*g - F*sin(theta) must stay >= 0 in every configuration; slider_controls (F<=60N, theta<=85deg) keep N>0 for all four authored pairs and every reachable sandbox setting
displacement is required for work: d=0 forces W=0 regardless of F (S2)
the perpendicular component F*sin(theta) does zero work on this flat floor at any theta; only F*cos(theta) enters W
static friction never exceeds mu_s*N; S2's ramp target (36 N) stays at 0.816 x maxStat (44.1 N), so the crate never breaks free
mass does not appear in W = F*d*cos(theta); a heavier crate takes longer to cover the same displacement, but the force does the identical work

aha_moment.statement: You can push with all your strength and do exactly zero work.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The F arrow ramps up to 36 N and the friction readout tracks it exactly, but the crate never moves and the work meter holds at 0.0 J throughout.

scene_composition.text: A steady pull moves the crate — the work meter climbs with the distance
at d = 1.00 m the meter reads 20.0 J — one newton through one metre is one joule
like pulling a loaded suitcase in a straight line along the floor

tts_sentences.text_en: A steady twenty newton pull moves the crate along the floor from rest.
As it speeds up, the work meter climbs with the distance moved.
When the crate has moved one metre, the meter reads twenty joules — one newton acting through one metre equals one joule.

STATE_2.title: A force with no motion does no work

scene_composition.text: The same pull, now against a rough floor that will not let go
F climbs to 36 N and friction matches it exactly — the crate never moves, the meter holds at 0.0 J
like pushing hard against a stalled car that does not move at all

tts_sentences.text_en: The same pull now acts on a crate resting on a rough floor.
The force grows larger and larger, and static friction balances it at every instant.
With zero displacement, the work meter holds at exactly zero joules, however large the pull becomes.

misconception_watch.belief: Pushing hard IS doing work — effort equals work, even if nothing moves.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The F arrow ramps large, the friction readout climbs to match it, the crate never moves, no d arrow ever appears, and the work meter holds exactly 0.0 J.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Work needs displacement — zero distance means zero work, whatever the force.

STATE_3.title: A tilted pull does less work

scene_composition.text: The same pull, now tilted upward at an angle above the floor
only the along-floor part of the pull does work — the meter climbs at half the rate of the flat pull
like pulling a suitcase by its slanted handle instead of pulling flat along the floor

tts_sentences.text_en: The same twenty newton pull now tilts upward at an angle.
The crate still slides across the floor, but the work meter climbs at half the rate per metre — only the part of the pull along the floor does any work.
Drag the angle slider and watch the meter's climb rate change live.

misconception_watch.belief: The whole force does work: W = F·d for any direction of pull.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The identical 20 N pull, tilted to 60°, buys only half the joules per metre — the arc shows the tilt, the full-length F arrow leans away from the motion, and the bar visibly climbs slower against the same growing d.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Tilting the pull leaves less of it pointing along the motion — the work per metre falls by cos θ.

STATE_4.title: Check the numbers: W = F·d·cos θ

scene_composition.text: A forty newton pull at sixty degrees, crossing a flag two metres along the floor
the formula predicts 40.0 J and the live meter reads 40.0 J at the same instant — prediction and measurement agree
the same check works for any steady pull at any angle

tts_sentences.text_en: A forty newton pull acts at sixty degrees on the same frictionless floor.
At the flag, two metres in, the formula predicts forty joules — the live meter reads the same forty joules at that instant.
This tilted pull does exactly as much work per metre as the first pull did.

STATE_5.title: W = F⃗·d⃗: two vectors give one number

scene_composition.text: A third pull, twenty newtons at thirty degrees, written as two vectors
W = F⃗ · d⃗ = F d cos θ — one number from the force arrow and the displacement arrow, at any angle
the same scalar product holds no matter how the pull is tilted

tts_sentences.text_en: A different pull now acts at a third angle: twenty newtons at thirty degrees.
The work formula becomes a scalar product of two arrows, force and displacement, collapsing into one number — force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them.
The same rule holds at any angle.

scene_composition.text: Change the force, the angle, or the mass, and drag the crate freely
W = F·d·cos θ — mass never appears in the formula
a heavier crate takes longer to move the same distance, but the force does the same work

tts_sentences.text_en: Mass does not appear in W = F·d·cos θ at all. A heavier crate takes longer to cover the same distance under the same pull, but the force does exactly the same work over that distance — try 2 kg and 8 kg at the same F and θ and watch the meter climb at the identical rate, just over a different time.

regeneration_variants.label: Pulling a Loaded Sled Across Packed Snow by an Angled Rope
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A loaded sled sits on packed snow. A rope runs from the sled up to shoulder height, so the pull tilts upward off the ground as it drags the sled forward.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical W = F·d·cos θ: only the component of the rope's pull along the snow moves the sled; the vertical part of the pull lightens the sled's contact with the snow without doing any work itself.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same single-body rig, same flat surface — only the labeled object changes from a crate to a sled and the pull is relabeled a rope.

regeneration_variants.label: Towing a Garden Wagon by Its Angled Handle
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A garden wagon is towed across a paved path by its long handle, held up at an angle rather than flat along the ground.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Same tilted-pull physics: the handle's angle sets cos θ, and only the along-the-path component of the tow does any work on the wagon.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same rig and physics — the crate is relabeled a wagon and the pull becomes the tow handle.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student who has mastered this concept can state that work requires both a force and a displacement along that force's direction; compute W = F·d·cos θ for any angle from 0° up to (not including) 90°; explain why a force with no displacement, or a force whose along-motion component is zero, does zero work; verify a live numeric prediction against a stamped measurement; write work as the scalar product W = F⃗·d⃗; and recognize that work done by a force is independent of the mass being moved.

questions.stem: A steady 60 N force pulls a crate 1.0 m across a frictionless floor, acting in the same direction the crate moves. How much work does the force do?

distractor_misconceptions.B: confuses work with a rate-like quantity that needs elapsed time to build up, instead of a product of force and displacement
distractor_misconceptions.C: adds the force value and the distance value instead of multiplying them (unit-blind arithmetic)
distractor_misconceptions.D: halves the product of force and distance, treating work like an average rather than a product

questions.tested_idea: W = F·d for a force aligned with the displacement; the joule as N·m
questions.parallel_form_stem: A gardener pulls a wheelbarrow with a steady 15 N force through 4 m, the force and the motion in the same direction. How much work is done?

questions.stem: A person pushes as hard as they can against a heavy filing cabinet that does not move at all, for several seconds. How much work does the push do on the cabinet?

options.A: Exactly 0 J, no matter how hard the push
options.B: A large positive value that grows the longer they push
options.C: A large positive value equal to the force times the cabinet's weight
options.D: A negative value, because the person gets tired

distractor_misconceptions.B: confuses effort and elapsed time with work — treats pushing hard for longer as accumulating work even with zero displacement
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses force with work and multiplies two force-like quantities together instead of using displacement
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses the person's own fatigue with the physics work done on the cabinet

questions.tested_idea: no displacement means zero work, regardless of how large the force is
questions.parallel_form_stem: A weightlifter holds a loaded barbell perfectly still overhead for ten seconds. How much work does the weightlifter's upward force do on the barbell during that time?

questions.stem: A 30 N force pulls a crate 5 m across a frictionless floor, directed 40° above the floor (cos 40° ≈ 0.77, sin 40° ≈ 0.64). How much work does the force do?

distractor_misconceptions.B: uses sin θ instead of cos θ — picks the component perpendicular to the motion instead of along it
distractor_misconceptions.C: uses the full force F·d and ignores the angle entirely
distractor_misconceptions.D: believes any tilt away from the direction of motion makes the work zero, not just a 90° tilt

questions.tested_idea: only the along-motion component F cos θ does work
questions.parallel_form_stem: A rope pulls a sled 8 m across level snow with a 25 N force directed 50° above the snow (cos 50° ≈ 0.64). How much work does the rope's pull do?

questions.stem: A 40 N force acts at 60° above a frictionless floor and pulls a crate 2.0 m along the floor (cos 60° = 0.5). How much work does the force do?

distractor_misconceptions.B: ignores cos θ entirely and uses the full F·d product
distractor_misconceptions.D: halves the correct answer, as if only half the force acted

questions.tested_idea: substituting real numbers into W = F·d·cos θ and checking it against a live measurement
questions.parallel_form_stem: A crate is pulled 10 m across a horizontal floor by a 50 N force directed 37° above the horizontal (cos 37° ≈ 0.80). Find the work done by the applied force.

questions.stem: Which expression correctly gives the work done by a constant force through a displacement, using vector notation?

options.A: W = F⃗ · d⃗ = F d cos θ
options.B: W = F⃗ × d⃗ = F d sin θ

distractor_misconceptions.B: confuses the dot product with the cross product, carrying the sin θ rule over from torque
distractor_misconceptions.C: adds the two vectors together instead of combining them into a scalar
distractor_misconceptions.D: adds the two vectors' magnitudes instead of taking their scalar product

questions.tested_idea: work is the scalar (dot) product of two vectors, not the cross product or a vector sum
questions.parallel_form_stem: Which of the following correctly names the mathematical operation that combines the force vector and the displacement vector to give work?

questions.stem: A 5 kg crate and an 8 kg crate are each pulled by the same steady 30 N force through the same 2 m displacement on a frictionless floor, in the direction of motion. How does the work done on the two crates compare?

options.A: Exactly the same for both — 60 J each
options.B: The 8 kg crate receives four times more work
options.C: The 5 kg crate receives more work because it accelerates faster
options.D: The work cannot be compared without knowing the time taken

distractor_misconceptions.B: invents a mass-scaling rule for work that does not exist — mass does not appear in W = F·d·cos θ at all
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses work with acceleration or speed, which DO depend on mass
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses work with power, which depends on time; work itself does not

questions.tested_idea: work done by a force is independent of the mass being moved
questions.parallel_form_stem: A 2 kg block and a 10 kg block are each pushed 3 m by the same 12 N force along a frictionless floor. Compare the work done on each block.
